questions: Is five sensors at 12 mm spacing enough resolution, or does the signal saturate or dead-zone at the tape edges?
Does the 0.06 m lookahead cause oscillation or overshoot, or does it help?
Is the 0.12 m track too narrow or too wide for turn-rate control at base speeds near 1.5 m/s?
Does any sensor read noise-dominated values (near 0 or 1 constantly)?
Any integration problems: sensor overlap, body clearance, or mass affecting traction?

intent: Establish a symmetric, mid-sized baseline: five 12 mm sensors at 12 mm spacing, 0.06 m ahead of the axle, on a 0.12 m track with 0.03 m wheels, a 0.12 m body and 0.8 kg mass. Suggested sensor_weights for the Integrator are [2, 1, 0, -1, -2] (positive x steers left). Purpose: obtain a clean first race and a first set of measurements to see whether sensor spacing, lookahead, or track width is the limiting factor.
learning: No prior evidence. Next iteration, compare line_loss_events, rms_error and max_error against the baseline to see whether lookahead or sensor count is the main limit before changing geometry.
rationale: Iteration 0 has no race telemetry and no Integrator feedback, so this proposal is a neutral baseline built from the contract. Five sensors are spread across the 0.08 m half-width limit, with 12 mm spacing. A 12 mm footprint at that spacing keeps adjacent sensors overlapping slightly, so the line is always seen by at least one sensor and the position estimate changes smoothly. The sensors sit 0.06 m ahead of the axle so the controller sees the line before the wheels reach it, which gives the controller room to act at speed. The wheel track is 0.12 m, a middle value that gives a reasonable turn rate without excess yaw inertia. The wheel radius is 0.03 m. The body is 0.12 m wide, which widens the off-track limit to about 0.09 m (tape half-width 0.0125 plus 0.03), so the robot is not ended early by brief excursions. Mass is 0.8 kg, low enough for quick acceleration and high enough for traction. Expected result: a completed run on the development tracks with modest line error. The suggested weights are proportional to sensor x, so a line on the left gives a positive (left-steering) signal. I expect the Integrator to tune gains; the weights are only a starting point.
